title: How do sealed classes/interfaces extend OOP's inheritance by giving the supertype CONTROL over its hierarchy (permits only listed subtypes, each must be final/sealed/non-sealed), and how does this enable exhaustive pattern matching in switch?
shortTitle: What are sealed classes and interfaces?
keyPoints: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend them using the permits clause
Each permitted subtype must be final (leaf), sealed (controlled further), or non-sealed (open: escape hatch)
The compiler knows all possible subtypes at compile time, enabling exhaustive pattern matching in switch
Exhaustive switch: no default needed; adding a new subtype causes compile errors everywhere it is not handled
Sealed plus records create algebraic data types: TransactionResult can only be Success, Failure, or Pending
Java 17 feature: complementary to records for building type-safe, exhaustive hierarchies

s1_definition.oneliner: Sealed means the parent controls which children exist via a permits list. Children must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. Enables exhaustive switch: compiler ensures all subtypes handled. Adding a new subtype causes compile errors everywhere.
s1_definition.profdef:
A `sealed` class or interface restricts which classes can extend or implement it using the `permits` clause.

- **permits clause**: `sealed interface PaymentChannel permits Neft, Upi, Rtgs` means only Neft, Upi, and Rtgs can implement PaymentChannel. Any other class gets a compile error.
- **Permitted subtypes** must be one of: `final` (no further extension, leaf node), `sealed` (controlled further extension), or `non-sealed` (open for anyone to extend, escape hatch).
- **Exhaustive pattern matching**: the compiler knows all possible subtypes at compile time. In a switch, no default is needed. If a new subtype is added to the permits list, every switch that does not handle it gets a compile error.
- **Sealed plus records**: creates algebraic data types where the type hierarchy is a closed set and every case is a record with named components.
s1_definition.analogy: Before sealed: the PaymentChannel interface at National Bank of India was open. Anyone could create BitcoinChannel implements PaymentChannel without the bank's approval. With sealed: PaymentChannel says only Neft, Upi, and Rtgs are approved channels. If someone tries to create BitcoinChannel, it is a compile error. Adding ImpsChannel to the permits list causes compile errors in every switch that does not handle it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  SEALED HIERARCHY
  ──────────────────────────────────────────

  sealed interface PaymentChannel
  permits NeftChannel, UpiChannel, RtgsChannel
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ PaymentChannel (sealed)       │
  │   permits:                    │
  │   ├── NeftChannel (final)     │
  │   ├── UpiChannel (final)      │
  │   └── RtgsChannel (final)     │
  │                               │
  │   BitcoinChannel -> COMPILE   │
  │                    ERROR      │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  EXHAUSTIVE SWITCH
  switch (channel) {
    case NeftChannel  -> handled
    case UpiChannel   -> handled
    case RtgsChannel  -> handled
    // No default needed.
    // Add ImpsChannel to permits
    // -> compile error HERE
  }

  SEALED + RECORDS = ALGEBRAIC DATA TYPE
  sealed interface TransactionResult
  ├── record Success(utr, amount)
  ├── record Failure(code, message)
  └── record Pending(refId, wait)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealed classes and interfaces (Java 17) give the supertype control over its hierarchy using the permits clause. Only listed subtypes can extend or implement the sealed type. Any other class gets a compile error. Each permitted subtype must be final (leaf), sealed (controlled further), or non-sealed (open escape hatch).

The key benefit is exhaustive pattern matching in switch (Java 21). The compiler knows all possible subtypes, verifies every case is handled, and no default clause is needed. Adding a new subtype (ImpsChannel) to the permits list causes compile errors in every switch statement that does not handle it: zero silent drops, zero missed cases.

Sealed plus records create algebraic data types: TransactionResult can only be Success, Failure, or Pending. The switch destructures each record type and handles it exhaustively. If the team adds a Timeout result type, every switch in the codebase immediately shows a compile error.

Remember one sentence: sealed types control which children can exist, enabling exhaustive pattern matching in switch where adding a new subtype causes compile errors everywhere it is not handled.
